title: Nines without end
hook: 0.999... looks a hair short of 1. Zoom in on the gap and try to find it.

doesNotKnow: that 0.999... names the same number as 1

misconception: 0.999... is a hair less than 1: there is a tiny gap, or a gap that shrinks forever without closing.
objective: The learner can explain that after n nines the gap to 1 is 0.00...01 (one tenth of the previous gap), so with all the nines the gap would have to be smaller than every such number; the only such non-negative number is 0, so 0.999... = 1.

claims.text: With n nines after the point, the gap to 1 is 0.00...01 with n - 1 zeros, that is 1/10^n; each extra nine cuts it to a tenth.
On the stage each new nine zooms in ten times on the gap, so the gap always fills the last tenth of the view.
claims.source: Stage design: the view after n nines spans [1 - 10^-(n-1), 1], ten times narrower than before, and the point 1 - 10^-n sits at 9/10 of it.

claims.text: A gap smaller than every one of 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, ... cannot be positive, so the gap between 0.999... and 1 is 0 and 0.999... = 1.
claims.source: Archimedean property: for any g > 0 there is n with 1/10^n < g. Equivalently the geometric series 9/10 + 9/100 + ... sums to (9/10) / (1 - 1/10) = 1. Any real-analysis text, e.g. Abbott, Understanding Analysis (2nd ed., 2015), sec. 1.4 and 2.7.

claims.text: Three times 0.333... is 0.999..., and three times 1/3 is 1.
claims.source: 1/3 = 0.333... (long division); multiplying each digit by 3 has no carries, giving 0.999...; 3 x 1/3 = 1.

recall.question: Is 0.4999... (nines forever after the 4) less than 0.5, or equal to it?
options: Less than 0.5 by a tiny amount
Less than 0.5 by an amount that keeps shrinking
recall.why: The gap would have to be smaller than 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001 and so on, all at once. Only 0 is, so 0.4999... = 0.5.
